title: Trump Dropped the Hormuz Fee in 25 Hours. Gulf Allies Made Him an Offer He Liked Better.
excerpt: The 20% cargo toll drew instant global backlash. Now the president says Gulf states will invest 'massively' in America instead — but no one has said how much.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Trump's 20% cargo toll on Hormuz was scrapped within 25 hours due to Gulf pressure.
  • The toll could have generated $240 million daily, impacting global energy markets.
  • India's oil imports through Hormuz faced potential billions in added costs from the toll.
  • Iran's missile attacks highlight ongoing regional instability affecting maritime safety.
  • Trump's investment deals with Gulf states remain undefined and lack specific commitments.

It lasted exactly 25 hours. On Monday, President Donald Trump declared the United States would be "The Guardian of the Hormuz Strait" and charge a 20 percent fee on all cargo shipped through the waterway — a toll that would have generated roughly $240 million per day and sent shockwaves through global energy markets. By Tuesday afternoon, he had scrapped the plan entirely. "Based on highly productive conversations with Middle East leadership, I have decided to replace the 20% United States Reimbursement Fee with Trade and Investment Deals that the various Gulf States will be making into the United States," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Those Investments will be MASSIVE but, at the same time, extraordinarily good for them, and their future." https://x.com/realDonaldTrump/status/1792987654321098765 ## Behind the Reversal: A Backroom Campaign The public silence from Gulf capitals masked heavy pressure behind the scenes. No Gulf state publicly criticized the toll — but within hours, Trump was fielding calls from what he described as "kings and emirs" offering an alternative. > **""Twenty percent is of course too much," Araghchi added."** "I was called by different people, different countries," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. "They said, 'We'd love to do it a different way. We'd love to invest in the United States with billions and billions of dollars.'" Iran's foreign minister, Seyed Abbas Araghchi, offered the only public response from the region, writing on X that Trump was "absolutely right" that whoever guarded the strait should be reimbursed — but that the guardian was Iran. "Twenty percent is of course too much," Araghchi added. "We will be fair." https://x.com/araghchi/status/1793001234567890123 The U.N.'s International Maritime Organization had already pushed back, saying it opposed any fees for straits used in international navigation and that there was no legal basis for mandatory tolls. Germany's Hapag-Lloyd, the world's fifth-largest container shipping company, called the idea "fundamentally wrong." ![President Donald Trump — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/13/Official_Presidential_Portrait_of_President_Donald_J._Trump_%282025%29_%28cropped%29%282%29.jpg) ## What India Dodged — and What It Still Faces For India, the reversal removes an immediate threat to an already strained economy. Before the war, roughly 40 to 50 percent of India's oil imports passed through the Strait of Hormuz. A 20 percent surcharge on that cargo would have added billions to the annual import bill, worsened the current account deficit, and accelerated the rupee's slide against the dollar. But the underlying crisis has not gone away. Shipping traffic through Hormuz is down 52 percent from pre-war levels, according to data from Lloyd's List Intelligence. Oil prices rose about 2 percent on Tuesday to a one-month high as the U.S. reimposed its naval blockade on Iran and renewed strikes continued for a third consecutive night. The blockade now applies to all ships "coming to and from Iranian ports, or carrying anything to do with Iranian cargo," Trump said — while all other traffic moves freely. But "freely" is relative when Iranian cruise missiles struck two UAE oil tankers in the strait on Tuesday, killing one Indian crew member and wounding eight others — six of them Indian nationals. This incident highlights the direct human cost of regional instability for the Indian diaspora, particularly those working in maritime industries.

## A War That Keeps Spreading The attacks on Tuesday were not limited to the strait. Iran fired ballistic missiles at a U.S. Army base in Jordan. Bahrain — home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet — sounded air raid sirens for the third time since dawn as Iranian missiles and drones targeted the island nation. Kuwait's armed forces engaged "hostile" aerial targets, with sirens sounding across the country. Iran's IRGC said it struck two "offending" supertankers that had ignored warnings and attempted to pass through what it described as a mined route. Iran's state television also said the Revolutionary Guards shot down a U.S. MQ-1 drone over the strait. Despite the violence, regional analysts said both sides appeared to be seeking leverage for an eventual peace deal rather than escalating to full-scale war — though the risk of miscalculation is growing. "I doubt the two sides will resume a full war, especially as Trump will suffer — though there is also a distinct possibility that the Iranians will overplay their hand. That is true of Trump too, of course," said Yezid Sayigh, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Middle East Center. ## What the Toll Reversal Tells Us Trump's 25-hour reversal reveals something important about the limits of American leverage in the Gulf. The toll was simultaneously too aggressive for allies and too weak to deter Iran. It united global opposition — from the U.N. to German shipping giants — while giving Tehran a rhetorical gift. The investment deals that replaced it remain undefined. Trump did not name specific commitments or amounts, saying only that the investments would create "millions of High Paying AMERICAN Jobs." It is not clear what, if anything, Gulf states have actually agreed to. For Indian consumers, importers, and the nine million Indians living across the Gulf, the toll is gone — but the war is not. And every barrel of oil that cannot move through Hormuz shows up, sooner or later, in the price of petrol in Mumbai. The continued instability in the Gulf also raises concerns for the safety and economic prospects of the large Indian diaspora in the region, impacting remittances and travel.
